result.summary: Ulysses sails to the edge of Oceanus and raises the dead with a blood offering. Teiresias foretells his journey home, and he speaks with his mother and with many famous women and heroes, including Agamemnon, Achilles and Hercules. Between the ghosts, the Phaeacians urge Alcinous to give generous gifts and ask Ulysses to go on.

scenes.title: Voyage and offering at Oceanus
scenes.summary: Ulysses and his crew sail to the land of the Cimmerians. He digs a trench, pours offerings and sacrifices the sheep, and the ghosts gather.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must reach the dead and keep them from the blood without losing his nerve.

place.name: land of the Cimmerians by Oceanus

scenes.title: Elpenor asks for burial
scenes.summary: The ghost of Elpenor tells how he died falling from Circe's roof and begs for burial. Ulysses promises.
scenes.stakes: Elpenor's unburied ghost may bring the gods' anger on Ulysses.

scenes.title: Teiresias' prophecy
scenes.summary: Teiresias drinks the blood and foretells the trouble from Neptune and the danger at Thrinacia. He also foretells the suitors' killing, the oar journey and a gentle death.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses' return, his ship, his men and his home depend on obeying the prophecy.

scenes.title: Ulysses and his mother
scenes.summary: Anticlea tells him of the situation at home and says she died of longing for him. He tries three times to embrace her but cannot. Then the ghosts of women gather.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses faces grief at losing his mother again and needs news of his household.

scenes.title: The catalogue of heroines
scenes.summary: Ulysses names the women he saw, among them Tyro, Antiope, Alcmena, Epicaste, Chloris, Leda, Iphimedeia and Ariadne, with brief tales of each.

scenes.title: Pause in the Phaeacian hall
scenes.summary: Ulysses offers to stop, but Arete and Alcinous press him to stay and continue. He agrees.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses' escort home and his gifts depend on the Phaeacians' goodwill.

scenes.title: Agamemnon's ghost
scenes.summary: Agamemnon tells how Aegisthus and Clytemnestra murdered him, and warns Ulysses to be wary of women. Ulysses cannot say whether Orestes lives.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses is warned about trusting Penelope at his homecoming.

scenes.title: Achilles and Ajax
scenes.summary: Achilles says he would rather be a living servant than king of the dead, and rejoices at news of Neoptolemus. Ajax, still angry over the armour, will not speak.
scenes.stakes: Ajax's unforgiven anger over the armour dispute remains.

scenes.title: Judges, sinners and Hercules
scenes.summary: Ulysses sees Minos, Orion, Tityus, Tantalus and Sisyphus, then Hercules' phantom. Frightened by the crowd of ghosts, he returns to the ship and sails.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses fears Proserpine sending the Gorgon's head against him.

notable_quotes.reason: Achilles says he would rather be a living servant than king among the dead.
Memorable image of Sisyphus's endless labour.
Agamemnon's bitter condemnation of Clytemnestra and women.

analysis.text: The descent shows the cost of heroism and the grim nature of death. Ghosts are mere shadows, and even Achilles values life above glory.
Prophecy and the dead's warnings, especially Agamemnon's, shape Ulysses' return and foreshadow Thrinacia and the suitors.

legacy.text: The nekyia influenced Virgil's Aeneid Book 6 and Dante's Inferno.
The punishments of Tantalus and Sisyphus gave the words 'tantalize' and 'Sisyphean'.

fun_facts.text: Ancient critics debated whether the prophecy of the oar (sentences 31-36 here, in brackets) was a later addition.

language_notes.text: Oceanus is the great river thought to encircle the world; the Cimmerians dwell at its edge, a land of perpetual darkness at the border of the dead.
A cubit is an ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip, about half a metre or eighteen inches.
'Feckless' here means weak and powerless; the ghosts are feeble shadows of the living.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld where the dead dwell.
'Unwaked' means unmourned: no wake, the traditional vigil and lament over a corpse, had been held for him.
'Limbo' here simply means the gloomy realm of the dead; the Aeaean island is Circe's home, Aeaea.
A barrow is a burial mound. An oar planted on it marks Elpenor as a sailor, a standard memorial in Homeric burial.
Theban means from Thebes, the Greek city where Teiresias lived as a famous blind seer.
Ulysses blinded the Cyclops Polyphemus, Neptune's son (told earlier in the story), which is the source of Neptune's grudge.
The Thrinacian island is Thrinacia, where the sun god's sacred flocks graze. The sun is Hyperion (Helios), who sees everything.
"By force or fraud" means openly in battle or by trickery; either way the suitors will die.
A winnowing shovel is a tool for tossing grain in the air to separate the chaff. The stranger will mistake the oar for one.
Hecatombs were large sacrifices, originally of a hundred oxen.
"Death shall come to you from the sea" is ambiguous: it may mean death away from the sea, or death coming from it.
Oceanus is the great river encircling the world in Greek thought; Ulysses has crossed it by ship to reach the land of the dead.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously; here, whether the gods gave her a gentle death.
"Magistrate" is a Victorian word for Telemachus's role as a prominent young man of rank in Ithaca, invited to feasts.
"In this wise" means "in this way"; the archaic phrase introduces her account of her death.
"Thrice" means three times; "touched to the quick" means deeply hurt in feeling.
"Anon" is archaic for "soon" or "presently".
"Deemed" means judged; he decides to hold back the ghosts with his sword so each drinks the blood in turn.
"Loosed her virgin girdle" is a euphemism: untying the girdle (belt) signals the loss of virginity.
"Rejoice in all good will" is a formal farewell-like greeting; "about this time twelve months" means a year from now.
The sense is that, despite their strength, they could not hold the city securely until it had a defensive wall.
Oedipodes is this translation's form of Oedipus; Epicaste is the Jocasta of later tragedy.
"Avenging spirits" are the Erinyes (Furies), who punished crimes against family, here the wrong done to a mother.
The unnamed seer is Melampus, who tried to steal the cattle for his brother Bias to win Pero as bride.
A fathom is about six feet and a cubit roughly eighteen inches, so the boys' size is enormously exaggerated.
Piling Ossa and Pelion on Olympus alludes to the giants' attempt to storm heaven; the brothers are Otus and Ephialtes.
Ariadne helped Theseus escape the Minotaur's labyrinth; he abandoned her on Dia, where Bacchus (Dionysus) had a claim on her.
"Enthralled" means held spellbound; the cloister is the roofed colonnade or hall where the Phaeacians sat listening.
"Niggardly" means stingy or miserly in giving.
"Redound greatly to my advantage" means it would bring me much benefit; "fuller-handed" means carrying more wealth and gifts.
A "charlatan" is a fraud who pretends to knowledge or credentials; here paired with "swindler" for a cheating liar.
"Argives" is a name for the Greeks generally, here those who fought at Troy; Alcinous asks about heroes who died there.
"Tasted the blood": the ghosts can speak and recognize the living only after drinking the sacrificial blood Ulysses poured out.
"Cattle-lifting or sheep-stealing" means raiding; cattle raids were a normal form of warfare and plunder in heroic society.
"Wedding breakfast, or picnic" are modern-sounding terms from this translation; the original refers to a feast or communal meal.
"Cloister" here means the covered colonnade or hall of the house where the banquet was held.
Not closing the dying man's eyes and mouth was a grave neglect of the duties owed to the dead.
Helen's flight with Paris caused the Trojan War, in which many Greeks died. She was Clytemnestra's sister.
"Steal a march upon them" means to arrive secretly, gaining an advantage by surprise.
Orchomenus, Pylos and Sparta are places where Orestes might have taken refuge. Menelaus, Agamemnon's brother, ruled Sparta.
Danaans, Argives and Achaeans are all Homer's names for the Greeks as a whole.
"Silly" here means feeble or helpless, not foolish; the dead are pitiable, powerless shades.
"Fleet descendant of Aeacus" refers to Achilles, whose father Peleus was Aeacus's son; "fleet" is his standing epithet for swiftness.
"Supersede" means to push aside from authority; Achilles fears Peleus may be dethroned in his old age.
"A woman's bribes" alludes to a gift to Eurypylus's mother, which induced him to fight at Troy. The Ceteians were his followers.
The horse is the wooden horse of Troy, built by Epeus, in which Greek leaders hid to take the city.
"Mars" is the war god; "the rage of Mars" means the chance fury of battle.
Achilles' armour was made by Hephaestus and given by his mother Thetis. Ulysses and Ajax competed for it after Achilles died.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld. The stray "97" is a footnote marker, not part of the text.
Asphodel is a pale flower of meadows, associated in Greek thought with the dead and the underworld.
Tityus attacked Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis, at Panopeus near Delphi (Pytho); his liver-eating punishment answers that crime.
"Dying to quench his thirst" is used literally here: he is desperate for water yet already dead, and never relieved.
"Whithers" is an archaic form meaning in every direction, to whatever place.
Hercules' last labour for Eurystheus was to bring Cerberus, the hound guarding Hades, up to the living world.
The Gorgon's head turned beholders to stone; Ulysses fears Proserpine (the Greek Persephone) might send it against him.
"Would fain have seen" means gladly would have seen, or eagerly wished to see.

context_notes.text: Circe is the goddess-sorceress of Aeaea who had detained Ulysses' crew for a year, then gave directions for reaching the dead.
Hades rules the underworld with his wife Proserpine (the Greek Persephone). Ghosts must drink blood to speak, so Ulysses holds them back until Teiresias, the prophet, has answered.
Greeks believed unburied dead could not rest and could bring divine anger on the living, so Elpenor's request is urgent.
Teiresias was a blind prophet whose knowledge persisted after death. His golden sceptre marks his authority.
Ghosts can speak truly only after drinking the blood of the sacrificed animals in the trench.
Hades is both the god of the dead and the name of his realm.
Teiresias was a blind Theban seer whose ghost Ulysses was told by Circe to consult about his journey home.
Proserpine (the Greek Persephone) is queen of the dead, wife of Hades.
Ghosts in the underworld can speak only after drinking the blood of the sacrificed animals Ulysses has poured out.
Enipeus was a river in Thessaly, worshipped as a river god.
Neptune is the Roman name for the sea god (Greek Poseidon); this translation uses Roman names for the gods.
Hercules was Alcmena's son by Jove; Megara was his wife.
Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, share immortality by alternating days between the underworld and the gods.
Eriphyle betrayed her husband Amphiaraus by accepting a golden necklace as a bribe.
Arete is Alcinous' wife and queen of the Phaeacians, held in unusual honor; Ulysses had been advised to seek her favor.
Echeneus is an elder Phaeacian statesman; his deference to Alcinous shows how the council worked.
The "wicked woman" is Clytemnestra, who helped murder Agamemnon on his return; the story follows in this book.
Proserpine (the Greek Persephone) is queen of the dead. Agamemnon was king of Mycenae and leader of the Greek forces at Troy.
Cassandra was a Trojan princess and prophetess, taken by Agamemnon as a war prize. She was killed along with him.
The house of Atreus, Agamemnon's family, was cursed by a history of betrayal and murder.
Telemachus was an infant when Ulysses left for Troy, so Agamemnon assumes the boy is now grown.
Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, was raised on Scyros. Ulysses fetched him to Troy after Achilles' death.
Ajax went mad after losing the contest and killed himself. Ulysses regrets that his victory caused this.
Minos, a legendary king of Crete, became a judge of the dead after dying.
Orion was a giant hunter; in the underworld he still pursues the beasts he killed in life.
Hercules was deified and dwells on Olympus, married to Hebe, goddess of youth; only his shade remains in Hades.
Hercules served Eurystheus, king of Tiryns and Mycenae, by Juno's scheming, performing twelve labours.

literary_notes.text: Mist, darkness and 'one long melancholy night' build a gloomy atmosphere that prepares for the entrance into the realm of the dead.
The list of ghosts (brides, bachelors, old men, maids, warriors) conveys the crowd and the universality of death, ending in the eerie screaming sound.
Ulysses' wry remark that the dead man outpaced his ship mixes grim humour with astonishment at Elpenor's swift journey.
Elpenor frankly blames his own drunkenness, painting himself as a humble, unlucky, rather foolish crewman.
Neptune's anger anticipates the storms and sufferings that will delay Ulysses' return.
The if-then warning sets up a choice for Ulysses and prepares the later disaster when his men slaughter the cattle.
The repeated "tell me" shows Ulysses' emotional urgency and tenderness toward his mother.
Laertes's rags and bed of leaves show his grief and neglect, conveying his suffering through concrete detail.
Anticlea dying of longing, not illness, makes Ulysses's absence a painful cost borne by those who love him.
The mother's ghost slipping away like a dream or phantom shows its insubstantial nature and Ulysses's frustrated grief.
The soul flitting away "as though it were a dream" explains the ghosts' unreachable, weightless state after death.
The wave arching like a mountain to hide the lovers gives the divine encounter a vivid, protective, almost supernatural setting.
Oedipodes acted unknowingly, so the tragedy lies in the gap between his ignorance and the truth later revealed by the gods.
The repeated nines and absurd measurements exaggerate the brothers' size to show their monstrous, heaven-defying nature.
"Hateful" sums up Eriphyle in one word, and the brisk line closes the catalogue with moral judgment.
Arete asserts her authority gently, claiming Ulysses as her guest while sharing the honor, showing her tact and influence.
Alcinous praises Ulysses' honesty, yet Ulysses is famous for clever deceptions; the reader may smile at the trust.
"Divine story" elevates Ulysses' tale to something inspired, like a bard's song.
Ulysses hints at a sadder tale of betrayal and death, preparing the reader for the stories of Agamemnon and others.
Agamemnon compares his killing to the slaughter of a fat beast and of animals for a feast, stressing the horror and indignity.
His bitter generalization about all women shows Agamemnon's anger and wounded pride, coloring his advice to Ulysses.
Agamemnon praises Penelope, yet readers know of the suitors in her house, so the warning and the reassurance both carry tension.
Ulysses' cautious, truthful reply shows his prudence and reluctance to speak without knowledge.
Ulysses' consolation that Achilles is a prince among the dead is rejected in the next lines, which makes it ring hollow.
The greatest hero prefers the humblest life to rule among the dead, overturning the heroic ideal of glory and showing Homer's bleak view of death.
Calling Ajax a "tower of strength" presents him as a defensive fortification for the Greek army.
Ajax's silent turning away embodies lasting resentment, a wound that death does not heal.
The "pitiless" stone seems to act with cruel will, intensifying the futility of Sisyphus' endless punishment.
Ghosts are compared to scared birds, conveying their helpless flitting panic around the fearsome hero.
Hercules' black look, ready bow and glaring eyes show him as perpetually the warrior, even as a phantom.
Hercules' pity for Ulysses, calling his life sorry, shows even the greatest hero shared hardship.
Ulysses' terror of Proserpine and the Gorgon's head signals the danger of staying, prompting his hasty departure.
